title: On the Impossibility of Separating Intelligence from Judgment: The Computational Intractability of Filtering for AI Alignment
claim: Safety cannot come from external filters wrapped around a powerful untrusted model; intelligence and judgment cannot be separated.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right chain, brain-in-a-vat flanked by two filters
description: A grayscale cartoon runs left to right. A red-outlined pink box reading 'Harm Inciting Prompt' feeds a pipe into a labeled 'FILTER MACHINE', a gauge-fitted canister. The pipe continues up and over into a glass cylinder holding a brain with gears, the untrusted AI as a brain in a vat. Another pipe leaves the top of the vat and goes down into a second 'FILTER MACHINE'. From there a pipe runs up to a pink 'Harmful Output' box at top right, which connects to a small friendly robot on the right who receives the command. The pink labels are the only color, so the eye goes to them and then to the central brain. The figure shows the filter-wrapped setup that the paper argues cannot work.
caption: This figure illustrates a potential filtering-based alignment system. A powerful, untrusted AI (the brain in a vat) is connected to two filters: a prompt filter (left) that blocks harmful inputs, and an output filter (right) that screens dangerous responses. Only prompt–output pairs that pass both filters are released into the world and get "executed", as shown by the robot receiving a command. The main message of the paper is that alignment can't be achieved in such a setup, i.e., alignment will not be achieved by separating "thinking/intelligence" (brain) from the "decision-making/judgment" (filters). Parts of the figure were generated with Sora [ref].
abstract: With the increased deployment of large language models (LLMs), one concern is their potential misuse for generating harmful content. Our work studies the alignment challenge, with a focus on filters to prevent the generation of unsafe information. Two natural points of intervention are the filtering of the input prompt before it reaches the model, and filtering the output after generation. Our main results demonstrate computational challenges in filtering both prompts and outputs. First, we show that there exist LLMs for which there are no efficient prompt filters: adversarial prompts that elicit harmful behavior can be easily constructed, which are computationally indistinguishable from benign prompts for any efficient filter. Our second main result identifies a natural setting in which output filtering is computationally intractable. All of our separation results are under cryptographic hardness assumptions. In addition to these core findings, we also formalize and study relaxed mitigation approaches, demonstrating further computational barriers. We conclude that safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights); in particular, black-box access to the LLM will not suffice. Based on our technical results, we argue that an aligned AI system's intelligence cannot be separated from its judgment.
